'''''Salvia elegans''''' is a [[perennial]] shrub native to Mexico. It has a number of variants, including '''pineapple sage''' and '''tangerine sage'''.<ref>[https://www.epicgardening.com/types-of-sage// Epic Gardening: Salvia Elegans]</ref>

==Description==
Pineapple sage is a [[short-day plant]] that produces numerous erect leafy stems up to {{Convert|150|cm}}. The leaves have an attractive scent that is similar to [[pineapple]]. The flowering season in Mexico is August onward; further north it may not flower until later autumn;<ref>[https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2002/oct/20/gardens / Monty Don: Sage concern]</ref> if there is no frost, it may flower until spring. It has tubular red flowers.

The variety 'Honey Melon', which has the same pineapple fragrance in the leaves, blooms early in the summer, rather than in autumn.<ref name="Clebsch">{{cite book |last1=Clebsch |first1=Betsy |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NM0iwB8GrQYC&dq=%22salvia+elegans%22&pg=PA115 |title=The New Book of Salvias |last2=Barner |first2=Carol D. |publisher=Timber Press |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-88192-560-9 |pages=115–117}}</ref>

Tangerine sage grows to about {{Convert|60–90|cm|abbr=on}} tall, has bronze edged leaves and a citrus scent. It is summer flowering.<ref>[https://langthorns.com/index.php?route=product/product&product_id=16986 / Langthorn's Plantery: Salvia Elegans Tangerine]</ref>

=== Phytochemistry ===
The essential oil of ''S. elegans'' consists primarily of [[caffeic acid]] and its derivatives, such as [[rosmarinic acid]] and [[salvianolic acid]], and [[flavones]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pereira |first1=Olívia R. |last2=Catarino |first2=Marcelo D. |last3=Afonso |first3=Andrea F. |last4=Silva |first4=Artur M. S. |last5=Cardoso |first5=Susana M. |year=2018 |title=''Salvia elegans'', ''Salvia greggii'' and ''Salvia officinalis'' Decoctions: Antioxidant Activities and Inhibition of Carbohydrate and Lipid Metabolic Enzymes |journal=Molecules |volume=23 |issue=12 |page=3169 |doi=10.3390/molecules23123169 |pmc=6321363 |pmid=30513773 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
Native to Mexico, the shrub inhabits [[Madrean pine–oak woodlands|Madrean]] and [[Mesoamerican pine–oak forests]] between {{convert|6000|and|9000|ft|abbr=on|order=flip}}.<ref name="Clebsch" />

== Ecology ==
The red tubular flowers are attractive to different species of [[hummingbird]]s, butterflies, bees, beetles, and flies, with hummingbirds being the primary pollinator.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal [[pollination syndrome]], having longer upper lips compared to the lower lips, is associated with other [[Ornithophily|ornithophilous]] species, believed to have been shaped over time by their primary |journal=Ecoscience |language=en |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=23–29 |doi=10.2980/1195-6860(2006)13[23:TDOFUB]2.0.CO;2 |issn=1195-6860|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Citation However, this morphological trait may promote a type of fertilization called [[geitonogamy]], as hummingbirds visit multiple flowers of the same plant.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cuevas |first1=E. |last2=Espino |first2=J. |last3=Marques |first3=I. |date=2018 |editor-last=Scopece |editor-first=G. |title=Reproductive isolation between Salvia elegans and S. fulgens, two hummingbird-pollinated sympatric sages |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/plb.12874 |journal=Plant Biology |language=en |volume=20 |issue=6 |pages=1075–1082 |doi=10.1111/plb.12874 |pmid=30004608 |bibcode=2018PlBio..20.1075C |issn=1435-8603}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=López-Segoviano |first1=Gabriel |last2=Arenas-Navarro |first2=Maribel |last3=Villa-Galaviz |first3=Edith |last4=Díaz-Infante |first4=Sergio |last5=Arizmendi |first5=María del Coro |date=2021-10-01 |title=Hummingbird-plant interactions along an altitudinal gradient in northwestern Mexico |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1146609X21000618 |journal=Acta Oecologica |volume=112 |article-number=103762 |doi=10.1016/j.actao.2021.103762 |bibcode=2021AcO...11203762L |issn=1146-609X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
[[File:Salvia_elegans,_Photo_by_Steve_Kerr.jpg|thumb|Salvia elegans, photo taken by Steve Kerr]]
''S. elegans'' displays incomplete dichogamy, where there is a slight temporal overlap between when the [[Stamen|anthers]] release pollen and when the [[Gynoecium|stigmas]] are receptive for pollen. In this species' case, the anthers develop pollen before their stigmas are receptive. While this strategy may allow for self pollination and possibly inbreeding depression, it mainly selects for [[allogamy]]. Inbreeding depression was not shown to occur for this species in one study in pre-germination stages. The display of incomplete dichogamy behavior may ensure for fruit and seed production when conditions are less ideal or when individuals are spread far apart from one another. The act of [[Autogamy|selfing]] is reduced by the flower's [[herkogamy]], where the stigma is located above the pollen filled anthers.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rosas-Guerrero |first1=Víctor |last2=Hernández |first2=Diego |last3=Cuevas |first3=Eduardo |date=2017 |title=Influence of pollen limitation and inbreeding depression in the maintenance of incomplete dichogamy in Salvia elegans |journal=Ecology and Evolution |language=en |volume=7 |issue=12 |pages=4129–4134 |doi=10.1002/ece3.2827 |doi-access=free |issn=2045-7758 |pmc=5478062 |pmid=28649325 |bibcode=2017EcoEv...7.4129R }}</ref>

== Cultivation ==
Pineapple sage was introduced into horticulture about 1870.<ref name="Clebsch" /> In cultivation, it typically reaches a height of {{Convert|1.2 to 1.5|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}}, with its roots spreading underground to form a large clump. The pale yellow-green leaves are veined and covered with fine hairs. Six to twelve scarlet flowers grow in whorls, featuring a long inflorescence that blooms gradually and lasts for an extended period. With a [[hard frost]], the plant will die down to the ground and grow back the following spring.<ref name="Clebsch" />

==Uses==
The leaves and flowers are edible.<ref>{{cite book |first=Beth |last=Hanson |title=Gourmet Herbs |year=2001 |publisher=Brooklyn Botanic Garden |isbn=978-1-889538-21-1 |page=[https://archive.org/details/gourmetherbsclas0000hans/page/90 90] |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/gourmetherbsclas0000hans/page/90 }}</ref> The plant is used in Mexican [[traditional medicine]], especially for anxiety and hypertension.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Herrera-Ruiza|first1=Maribel|last2=García-Beltrána|first2=Yolanda|last3=Morab|first3=Sergio|last4=Díaz-Véliz|first4=Gabriela|last5=Vianac|first5=Glauce S.B.|last6=Tortorielloa|first6=Jaime|last7=Ramíreza|first7=Guillermo|date=Aug 2006|title=Antidepressant and anxiolytic effects of hydroalcoholic extract from Salvia elegans|journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology|volume=107|issue=1|doi=10.1016/j.jep.2006.02.003|pmid=16530995|pages=53–8}}</ref>
